text: Spare in thy Youth, leſt Age ſhould find thee poor, When Time is paſt, and thou canſt ſpare no more: No coupled Miſery ſo great as either, As Age and Want, when both do meet together.
title: The New art of thriving, or, The Way to get and keep money being a seasonable caution against the extravagoncies of these times : containing sixteen excellent rules and observations for promoting good

text: Above all, to thrive, be very punctual in your Accounts: regiſter all Receipts and Diſburſements, and often delight to ballance them; never contemn little Advantages, nor ſlight ſmall Expences.
title: The New art of thriving, or, The Way to get and keep money being a seasonable caution against the extravagoncies of these times : containing sixteen excellent rules and observations for promoting good

text: The Scotch Proverb ſays well, Every little makes a mickle; and the Wiſe Man tells you plainly, He that deſpiſeth a little ſhall fall by little and little.
title: The New art of thriving, or, The Way to get and keep money being a seasonable caution against the extravagoncies of these times : containing sixteen excellent rules and observations for promoting good

text: The ſerious Spaniard, when he would beſtow the bittereſt Curſe upon an Enemy, is wont to wiſh, He may be a Beggar when he is old.
title: The New art of thriving, or, The Way to get and keep money being a seasonable caution against the extravagoncies of these times : containing sixteen excellent rules and observations for promoting good

text: Suretiſhip has been an eminent Gulph to ſwallow fair Eſtates; ſo much the more lamentable, becauſe it falls upon Perſons of the beſt Nature, eaſily enveigled by crafty Knaves to engage for their own Debts, which they never deſign to pay themſelves.
title: The New art of thriving, or, The Way to get and keep money being a seasonable caution against the extravagoncies of these times : containing sixteen excellent rules and observations for promoting good

text: Theſe Leſſons approved, if wiſely ye note, May ſave and advantage you many a Groat; Which if you can follow, Occaſion found, Then every Leſſon may ſave thee a Pound.
title: The New art of thriving, or, The Way to get and keep money being a seasonable caution against the extravagoncies of these times : containing sixteen excellent rules and observations for promoting good

text: Hear old Tuſſer on the Point: The Care of the Huſbandman enricheth the Hutch, The Eye of the Houſewife availeth as much.
title: The New art of thriving, or, The Way to get and keep money being a seasonable caution against the extravagoncies of these times : containing sixteen excellent rules and observations for promoting good

text: As to the Choice of a Wife, having little Experience myſelf, let me adviſe you in the Words of the ſame Poet, Tho' Love in chuſing far better than Gold, Let Love come with ſomewhat, the better to hold.
title: The New art of thriving, or, The Way to get and keep money being a seasonable caution against the extravagoncies of these times : containing sixteen excellent rules and observations for promoting good

text: Yet ſince Love is a Flame, it is convenient to have Fuel of an Eſtate, leſt the Damps of Neceſſity ſhould extinguiſh it.
title: The New art of thriving, or, The Way to get and keep money being a seasonable caution against the extravagoncies of these times : containing sixteen excellent rules and observations for promoting good

text: 'Tis the moſt critical Action of a Man's Life; not only his own Happineſs or Ruin, but his Relations and Poſterity are concerned in it; and ſince it can be done but once, it concerns us to conſider more than twice before we undertake it.
title: The New art of thriving, or, The Way to get and keep money being a seasonable caution against the extravagoncies of these times : containing sixteen excellent rules and observations for promoting good

text: What with Idleneſs, Waſte, and Embezzlements, he will find a ſenſible Conſumption in his Eſtate, if he do not well examine their Accounts, and continually inſpect their Doings.
title: The New art of thriving, or, The Way to get and keep money being a seasonable caution against the extravagoncies of these times : containing sixteen excellent rules and observations for promoting good

text: Can our beſt-ſtudied Faſhionmongers tell us what uſe there is of Perriwigs of ſix, ſeven, or eight, nay twenty or thirty Pounds a Wig; or of daubing of Coats or Petticoats with Silver Lace?
title: The New art of thriving, or, The Way to get and keep money being a seasonable caution against the extravagoncies of these times : containing sixteen excellent rules and observations for promoting good

text: No leſs vain is Extravagancy in ordinary Houſe keeping; the Variety of Diſhes does but oppreſs Nature and diſturb Digeſtion.

text: The Father Martyr'd, and the Son Miſled By Counſels of a Land to which he fled, As taught to Govern he forgot to Rule, And held the Reins not Temperate or Cool.
author: Dennis, John, 1657-1734.
title: The reverse: or, the tables turn'd A poem written in answer, paragraph by paragraph, to a late scurrilous and malicious medly of rhimes called the foreigners.

text: Let her indeed beware, and truly dread The Miſchiefs which are falling on her Head, Whilſt ſhe permits Audacious Slaves, to dare That Providence, that made Her Kings its Care; And lets a Servile Wretch for Servile Ends Traduce Her Monarch, and Defame his Friends.
author: Dennis, John, 1657-1734.
title: The reverse: or, the tables turn'd A poem written in answer, paragraph by paragraph, to a late scurrilous and malicious medly of rhimes called the foreigners.

text: When her High-Prieſts ſit inſolent in State, And grumble at the Pow'rs that made 'em great, Though from Agrippa's Bounty they are rais'd, To wear that Veſt which they before diſprais'd; When ev'n HALLASTIR's Gratitude is ſhown, In wiſhing for the Fall of Iſrael's Throne.
author: Dennis, John, 1657-1734.
title: The reverse: or, the tables turn'd A poem written in answer, paragraph by paragraph, to a late scurrilous and malicious medly of rhimes called the foreigners.

text: But ſtill reſolv'd to ſplit on Foreing Shelves, Rather than venture once to truſt themſelves, To Foreign Courts and Councils do reſort, To find a King their Freedom to ſupport.
author: Dennis, John, 1657-1734.
title: The reverse: or, the tables turn'd A poem written in answer, paragraph by paragraph, to a late scurrilous and malicious medly of rhimes called the foreigners.

text: But Wealth nor Peace could Conſecrate his Reign, Her Childrens Bleſſing was her Childrens Pain; Who in requital to the Race H' had run, Return'd his Goodneſs with a Martyr'd Son.
author: Dennis, John, 1657-1734.
title: The reverse: or, the tables turn'd A poem written in answer, paragraph by paragraph, to a late scurrilous and malicious medly of rhimes called the foreigners.

text: Their Land as if aſham'd their Crimes to ſee, Dives down beneath the ſurface of the Sea, Neptune, the God who do's the Seas command, Ne'er ſtands on Tip-toe to diſcry their Land?
author: Dennis, John, 1657-1734.
title: The reverse: or, the tables turn'd A poem written in answer, paragraph by paragraph, to a late scurrilous and malicious medly of rhimes called the foreigners.

text: Curs'd be the Pen, that dares ſuch Worth defame, And give that Murd'rous Fact a Glorious Name, Which Deaf to Pity, ſcatters it's Applauſe On what muſt Damn the Praiſer with the Cauſe.
author: Dennis, John, 1657-1734.
title: The reverse: or, the tables turn'd A poem written in answer, paragraph by paragraph, to a late scurrilous and malicious medly of rhimes called the foreigners.

text: Yet thoſe who Sav'd and Counſel'd us in War, Muſt not in Peace at Council Board appear, But in return for Conqueſt, take Diſgrace, And Naturaliz'd, not have a Natives Place.
author: Dennis, John, 1657-1734.
title: The reverse: or, the tables turn'd A poem written in answer, paragraph by paragraph, to a late scurrilous and malicious medly of rhimes called the foreigners.

text: If Iſrael's People could a Monarch chuſe, A living King at the ſame time refuſe; That Hiram's People, ſhall it e'er be ſaid, Have not the Right of Choice when he is Dead?
author: Dennis, John, 1657-1734.
title: The reverse: or, the tables turn'd A poem written in answer, paragraph by paragraph, to a late scurrilous and malicious medly of rhimes called the foreigners.

text: Iſrael, let it not in Gath be known, Nor let thy Gratitude reach Askalon, Publiſh it not, leaſt Heathens know thy ſhame, And Philiſtin's deride thy Sacred Name!
author: Dennis, John, 1657-1734.
title: The reverse: or, the tables turn'd A poem written in answer, paragraph by paragraph, to a late scurrilous and malicious medly of rhimes called the foreigners.

text: Proceed, my Muſe, the Story next relate Of Keppech, the imperious Chit of State, Mounted to Grandeur by the uſual Courſe, Of Whoring, Pimping, or a Crime that's worſe; Of Foreign Birth, and undeſcended too, Yet he like Bentir mighty Feats can do.
author: Dennis, John, 1657-1734.
title: The reverse: or, the tables turn'd A poem written in answer, paragraph by paragraph, to a late scurrilous and malicious medly of rhimes called the foreigners.

text: Yet Senſe of native Freedom ſtill remains, They fret and grumble underneath their Chains; Incens'd, enrag'd, their Paſſion does ariſe, Till at his Palace-Gate their Monarch dies.
author: Dennis, John, 1657-1734.
title: The reverse: or, the tables turn'd A poem written in answer, paragraph by paragraph, to a late scurrilous and malicious medly of rhimes called the foreigners.

text: Yet for the Language is the Man diſpis'd, Whilſt he that has no Thoughts is ador'd and priz'd. Beaſt, as thou art, impertinent in wrong, Thou need'ſt no Eve to Damn Thee but thy Tongue; Thy canker'd Malice, and thy feſter'd Thoughts Can turn the pureſt Vertues into Faults.
author: Dennis, John, 1657-1734.
title: The reverse: or, the tables turn'd A poem written in answer, paragraph by paragraph, to a late scurrilous and malicious medly of rhimes called the foreigners.

text: But now on this Day, both You and We, are to think of other Methods, for the procuring Succeſs to our Affairs.
author: Sharp, John, 1645-1714.
title: Fifteen sermons preach'd on several occasions the last of which was never before printed / by ... John, Lord Arch-Bishop of York ...

text: It is true indeed, a ſenſual Man hath no notion of this kind of pleaſures, no more than a Beaſt hath of the pleaſures of a Man.
author: Sharp, John, 1645-1714.
title: Fifteen sermons preach'd on several occasions the last of which was never before printed / by ... John, Lord Arch-Bishop of York ...

text: And not only ſo, but in our ſeveral Places and Stations, promoting Peace, and Unity and Concord among Chriſtians, and contributing what we can to the healing the ſad Breaches and Diviſions of our Nation.
author: Sharp, John, 1645-1714.
title: Fifteen sermons preach'd on several occasions the last of which was never before printed / by ... John, Lord Arch-Bishop of York ...

text: But I have this ſatisfaction, that I have ſincerely endeavoured in all my Preaching, to inſtruct you in the true Doctrine of the Goſpel, and to teach you the right way that leads to Salvation.
author: Sharp, John, 1645-1714.
title: Fifteen sermons preach'd on several occasions the last of which was never before printed / by ... John, Lord Arch-Bishop of York ...

text: But then it is to be conſidered, that this is not to be charged upon Vertue and Religion, but is the particular Fault of the Perſons.
author: Sharp, John, 1645-1714.
title: Fifteen sermons preach'd on several occasions the last of which was never before printed / by ... John, Lord Arch-Bishop of York ...

text: Let us every day call our Family together, and pay our Common Tribute of Prayer and Praiſe for the Mercies we do daily receive in common.
author: Sharp, John, 1645-1714.
title: Fifteen sermons preach'd on several occasions the last of which was never before printed / by ... John, Lord Arch-Bishop of York ...

text: All that remains now is, to make ſome brief Application of my Text, with reference to the buſineſs of the Day.
author: Sharp, John, 1645-1714.
title: Fifteen sermons preach'd on several occasions the last of which was never before printed / by ... John, Lord Arch-Bishop of York ...

text: And leaſt any one ſhould fear the Divine Juſtice, upon account that there is no ſatisfaction made to it for his Sins: Our Lord hath taken care to remove that Objection.
author: Sharp, John, 1645-1714.
title: Fifteen sermons preach'd on several occasions the last of which was never before printed / by ... John, Lord Arch-Bishop of York ...

text: And that God whoſe Care and Providence doth ſo particularly extend to every individual Man, that (as the ſame our Lord Jeſus ſpeaks) the very Hairs of our Head are numbered by him.
author: Sharp, John, 1645-1714.
title: Fifteen sermons preach'd on several occasions the last of which was never before printed / by ... John, Lord Arch-Bishop of York ...

text: He finds his way eaſily, when other Men are quite bewildred; and he readily expedites himſelf out of ſuch difficulties as thoſe that act by other principles find themſelves grievouſly intangled with.
author: Sharp, John, 1645-1714.
title: Fifteen sermons preach'd on several occasions the last of which was never before printed / by ... John, Lord Arch-Bishop of York ...

text: And every ſuch Man in particular reaps the benefit of ſuch his Endeavours; for he ſhares in his own Perſon that protection and ſecurity he procures to the Community.
author: Sharp, John, 1645-1714.
title: Fifteen sermons preach'd on several occasions the last of which was never before printed / by ... John, Lord Arch-Bishop of York ...

text: Who was believed in by the Patriarchs; Typified by the Law; Foretold by all the Prophets; Shadowed out in all the Oeconomy of the Jewiſh Nation; Expected by all the Iſraelites; And wiſhed for by the beſt of the Heathen World.
author: Sharp, John, 1645-1714.
title: Fifteen sermons preach'd on several occasions the last of which was never before printed / by ... John, Lord Arch-Bishop of York ...

text: God open our Eyes, that we may in this our day underſtand the Things that belong to Peace, before they be hid from our Eyes.
author: Sharp, John, 1645-1714.
title: Fifteen sermons preach'd on several occasions the last of which was never before printed / by ... John, Lord Arch-Bishop of York ...

text: For, ſaith he, I remain Conſtant to my former Principles, with reſpect to theſe great Doctrines of the Chriſtian Faith.
author: Field, John, 1652-1723.
title: The Christianity of the people called Quakers asserted, by George Keith: in answer to a sheet, called, A serious call to the Quakers, Attested by eight priests of the Church of England ... and affirme

text: The Poſtſ. alſo ſaith, They, the Quakers, do allow doing Servile Work on the Lord's-Day.
author: Field, John, 1652-1723.
title: The Christianity of the people called Quakers asserted, by George Keith: in answer to a sheet, called, A serious call to the Quakers, Attested by eight priests of the Church of England ... and affirme

text: In the ſaid Sheet it's ſaid, They (that is the Quakers) deny the Reſurrection of the Body after Death.
author: Field, John, 1652-1723.
title: The Christianity of the people called Quakers asserted, by George Keith: in answer to a sheet, called, A serious call to the Quakers, Attested by eight priests of the Church of England ... and affirme

text: This is no great Riddle nor Paradox to the leaſt Child of the New Jeruſalem; Paul indeed was before in Heaven, and ſo is every Regenerate Man at preſent.
author: Field, John, 1652-1723.
title: The Christianity of the people called Quakers asserted, by George Keith: in answer to a sheet, called, A serious call to the Quakers, Attested by eight priests of the Church of England ... and affirme

text: And Paul, writing concerning the Reſurrection of the Dead, ſaith, That is not firſt which is Spiritual, but that which is Natural (or Animal, and afterward that which is Spiritual) 1 Cor. 15.46.
author: Field, John, 1652-1723.
title: The Christianity of the people called Quakers asserted, by George Keith: in answer to a sheet, called, A serious call to the Quakers, Attested by eight priests of the Church of England ... and affirme

text: G. K. ſaith, Concerning that ye call your Chriſtian-Sabbath, which ye ſay is the Firſt Day of the Week, —but ye bring no ſober Proof for any ſuch Change, and the Scriptures ye cite ſay no ſuch thing, as Gen. 2.2, 3.
author: Field, John, 1652-1723.
title: The Christianity of the people called Quakers asserted, by George Keith: in answer to a sheet, called, A serious call to the Quakers, Attested by eight priests of the Church of England ... and affirme

text: For all God's Commands and Precepts, eſpecially of Publick Inſtitution, relating to the Church, are expreſs, in ſo many expreſs Words, and are not left to be gathered by uncertain and doubtful Conſequences.
author: Field, John, 1652-1723.
title: The Christianity of the people called Quakers asserted, by George Keith: in answer to a sheet, called, A serious call to the Quakers, Attested by eight priests of the Church of England ... and affirme

text: This is alſo a moſt falſe Charge, which they can never prove: But becauſe we deny their Carnal Conceptions of the Reſurrection, and hold us to Scripture-words, which is moſt ſafe, therefore they have ſo be-lyed us.
author: Field, John, 1652-1723.
title: The Christianity of the people called Quakers asserted, by George Keith: in answer to a sheet, called, A serious call to the Quakers, Attested by eight priests of the Church of England ... and affirme

text: G. K. ſaith, By W. Penn's words, it is clear to prove the contrary, of a Carnal Reſurrection.
author: Field, John, 1652-1723.
title: The Christianity of the people called Quakers asserted, by George Keith: in answer to a sheet, called, A serious call to the Quakers, Attested by eight priests of the Church of England ... and affirme

text: And are the ſo called Doctors, and Rectors, and thoſe that abet him, to be commended for their Wiſdom?
author: Field, John, 1652-1723.
title: The Christianity of the people called Quakers asserted, by George Keith: in answer to a sheet, called, A serious call to the Quakers, Attested by eight priests of the Church of England ... and affirme

text: How unreaſonable this Conſequence is, I leave unto ſober Men to Judge; as to Conclude, becauſe Men are Infallible, that therefore the Dictate and Light of God's Spirit in Men is Fallible alſo; Was not Peter Fallible in ſome Caſes?
author: Field, John, 1652-1723.
title: The Christianity of the people called Quakers asserted, by George Keith: in answer to a sheet, called, A serious call to the Quakers, Attested by eight priests of the Church of England ... and affirme

text: I do ſeriouſly and truly tell thee, as I faithfully believe that Chriſt did locally Aſcend upwards into the Heavens, whence alſo he ſhall Deſcend at the time of the Reſtitution of all things.
author: Field, John, 1652-1723.
title: The Christianity of the people called Quakers asserted, by George Keith: in answer to a sheet, called, A serious call to the Quakers, Attested by eight priests of the Church of England ... and affirme

text: And will he now ſay, Only the bare Writing or Characters, conſiſting of Ink and Paper, is properly the Word of God, and are Infallible, Divine, and not Humane?
author: Field, John, 1652-1723.
title: The Christianity of the people called Quakers asserted, by George Keith: in answer to a sheet, called, A serious call to the Quakers, Attested by eight priests of the Church of England ... and affirme

text: MOST ages have produced some shining models of undaunted virtue and unabating patriotism.—It is the part of the Biographer to select characters from the mass of mankind, and to hold those only up to view who have been most distinguished on the vast theatre of human life.
author: Cradock, Joseph, 1742-1826.
title: The life of John Wilkes, Esq: in the manner of Plutarch. Being a specimen of a larger work.

text: But fearing some Creditors, and having suffered in a Duel, he travelled into France with many other great men, for the recovery of his health and fortune.
author: Cradock, Joseph, 1742-1826.
title: The life of John Wilkes, Esq: in the manner of Plutarch. Being a specimen of a larger work.

text: But the never-to-be-forgotten work was the North Briton, or rather the No 45 of that celebrated paper, written by the late Reverend Mr. Churchill, and containing many spirited attacks against government, which not being well received, a process was preferred against the author.
author: Cradock, Joseph, 1742-1826.
title: The life of John Wilkes, Esq: in the manner of Plutarch. Being a specimen of a larger work.

text: Mr. Wilkes being never likely to have a more fair or honourable introduction to glory, generously declared the paper to be his own, —defied all government, and has been admired and rewarded for it.
author: Cradock, Joseph, 1742-1826.
title: The life of John Wilkes, Esq: in the manner of Plutarch. Being a specimen of a larger work.

text: FEAR'D by his Foes, by his Allies caress'd, Lov'd by his GOD, and by his People bless'd; Remain'd there ought to fear?
author: Wallis, John, 1714-1793.
title: The history of David's troubles: or, human frailty delineated. A sacred poem.

text: To the King's View her Snowy Charms were bare, He saw Her naked, and he own'd her Fair.
author: Wallis, John, 1714-1793.
title: The history of David's troubles: or, human frailty delineated. A sacred poem.

text: The thirsted Blood still sought he to attain By Fraud, by Force; but Fraud and Force were vain.
author: Wallis, John, 1714-1793.
title: The history of David's troubles: or, human frailty delineated. A sacred poem.

text: Murder'd he fell, who ill aspir'd to rule, A Traitor's Victim, and a Party's Tool!
author: Wallis, John, 1714-1793.
title: The history of David's troubles: or, human frailty delineated. A sacred poem.

text: Bethink, O King! for what hast Thou resign'd, Thy Peace, thy sweet Serenity of Mind; And Raptures which the Virtuous Soul bestow'd, Conscious of Worth, and conversant with GOD?
author: Wallis, John, 1714-1793.
title: The history of David's troubles: or, human frailty delineated. A sacred poem.

text: Nought fear'd He from Himself, nor understood David was yet by David unsubdu'd. Now was the Hour ill-fated he must know That vicious Pleasures terminate in Woe.
author: Wallis, John, 1714-1793.
title: The history of David's troubles: or, human frailty delineated. A sacred poem.

text: NE'ER felt his Soul the sad Effects of Sin, For all was pure, and all was calm within.
author: Wallis, John, 1714-1793.
title: The history of David's troubles: or, human frailty delineated. A sacred poem.

text: FARTHER, He saw him destin'd to sustain A deeper Anguish, and a keener Pain; When summon'd by the unrelenting Seer To the sad Choice of Famine, Plague, or War.
author: Wallis, John, 1714-1793.
title: The history of David's troubles: or, human frailty delineated. A sacred poem.

text: THE Seer, stern Anger frowning on his Brow, Reply'd;— The Man, whom Thou condemn'st, art THOU.
author: Wallis, John, 1714-1793.
title: The history of David's troubles: or, human frailty delineated. A sacred poem.

text: Rash Amnon's Death by Absolom decreed, For beauteous Tamar's violated Bed, And DAVID grieving at the impious Deed.
author: Wallis, John, 1714-1793.
title: The history of David's troubles: or, human frailty delineated. A sacred poem.

text: Inly the Fortunes of the King he mourn'd, Restrain'd the rising Grief, and Home return'd. While David in th' expiring Child beheld The sad Prediction of the Seer fulfill'd. Apart in Bitterness of Soul He sate, And his Repentance, as his Crime, was great.
author: Wallis, John, 1714-1793.
title: The history of David's troubles: or, human frailty delineated. A sacred poem.

text: Strict He enjoin'd, till by the Foes beset, Then to retire, and leave Him to his Fate.
author: Wallis, John, 1714-1793.
title: The history of David's troubles: or, human frailty delineated. A sacred poem.

text: He rose, the rash Resolve to JOAB wrote, Beneath whose Care His Hosts at Rabbah fought, To place Him where the surest Danger lay, In the sharp Conflict of the Doubtful Day.
author: Wallis, John, 1714-1793.
title: The history of David's troubles: or, human frailty delineated. A sacred poem.

text: Nay, further, to encrease your wretched State, Shall write in praise of Bailiffs, whom you hate, And humbly, in your Poems, stile 'em Good and Great.
author: Ward, Edward, 1667-1731.
title: A journey to Hell, or, A visit paid to the Devil a poem.

text: The Poor they promis'd should have Med'cines free, Instead of that the Upper-World may see, They make 'em pay great Rates for as bad Goods as we.
author: Ward, Edward, 1667-1731.
title: A journey to Hell, or, A visit paid to the Devil a poem.

text: Thus did the Partial Criticks all run Mad, And fiercely strugl'd for what neither had; As Whores their Reputations oft defend, And for a Good Name, which they want, contend; Whilst ev'ry stander-by the Feud derides, Takes neither part, but ridicules both sides.
author: Ward, Edward, 1667-1731.
title: A journey to Hell, or, A visit paid to the Devil a poem.

text: The Judge sum'd up, in a short Speech, their Sins, And then the Culprits Doom he thus begins.
author: Ward, Edward, 1667-1731.
title: A journey to Hell, or, A visit paid to the Devil a poem.

text: Some about preference of Wit fell out, And made a Riot in the Rhiming Rout, Wounding each other with Poetick Darts, And rail'd like Billingsgates to show their Parts; Each envious Wasp stung t'other at no rate, Expressing not his Judgment, but his Hate.
author: Ward, Edward, 1667-1731.
title: A journey to Hell, or, A visit paid to the Devil a poem.

text: The Judge arising did his Task assume, And gravely standing thus pronounc'd their Doom: Altho', says he, in diff'rent Robes you came, I find your Ills are equally the same: I decree therefore you alike shall feel, A Tythe of all the Punishments in Hell.
author: Ward, Edward, 1667-1731.
title: A journey to Hell, or, A visit paid to the Devil a poem.

text: Some with two Talents were profusely blest, And seem'd to study least, what they profest, In earnest Poetry, and Physick but in jest.
author: Ward, Edward, 1667-1731.
title: A journey to Hell, or, A visit paid to the Devil a poem.

text: Whence can you boast your Knowledge, lest you own, By study of your Files you're Learned grown?
author: Ward, Edward, 1667-1731.
title: A journey to Hell, or, A visit paid to the Devil a poem.

text: And when they'd rais'd their Lust by luscious Food, To bless with more encrease the Pious Brood, And kiss the Godly Dame was held divinely Good.
author: Ward, Edward, 1667-1731.
title: A journey to Hell, or, A visit paid to the Devil a poem.

text: Thus you at first were neither more nor less, Than servile Pedlars to the fruitful Press; No Copies cou'd ye buy, no Charter boast, But now alas, those good old Times are lost.
author: Ward, Edward, 1667-1731.

title: The Spanish descent. A poem. By the author of The true-born Englishman:

text: Why, the first law of Nature:—We take our own Pay— And next on our Friends a few Pensions bestow— And to you we apply when our Treasure runs low.
author: Spence, Thomas, 1750-1814.
title: Burke's address to the "swinish*" multitude! Tune "Derry down, down,"

text: At Corruption and Taxes, they never repine: If we only Proclaim, "YE ARE HAPPY!"—They say "WE ARE Happy!"—Believe and be Happy as they!

text: Nor dare to look out, if a KING passes by: Get ye down! down! down!—Keep ye down!

text: Be contented with that—and no more of your rout: Or a new Proclamation shall muzzle your Snout!

text: Yet remember I told you with caution to peep, For Swine at a distance WE prudently keep— Get ye down! &c.

text: But if he has no Knowledge of those Times, he is under a vast Uncertainty in every Patient; neither does he know whose Cure or Death he is carrying on with the greatest Assurance, tho' he Practice with the best Med'cine.

text: But also, for not having a true Theory of Diseases, we do not know when it is time to put a stop to our Successful Method; and but too frequently carry on a needless Practice, to the great Detriment and Hazard of the sick Person.

text: And therefore let any One who pretends to be familiarly acquainted with this Pacifick Med'cine, examine himself throughly by the Rules I have laid down, and rest satisfied with nothing less than his being qualified by the First.

text: THE World, I know, will admire what Merit of yours should obtain you this Address; but their Curiosity will be satisfied when they are told, that your Pretences on this Head are very great and singular.

text: But if you have any tolerating Method whereby you wou'd justifie your administring Med'cines in your Probation Time, do as you wou'd be done by; share your Freedom to others of your Brethren, who are at least in no lower a form of knowing than you be.

text: But if the Danger that possibly may come by it was ever imagin'd, how equal might the Dispute prove about taking of it on any of the mentioned Designs; but especially if the Operation of this Med'cine shou'd fall short of it; nay, if the contrary Effects were ever suppos'd to happen.

text: Now since there is so manifest Uncertainty in the Practice of this Excellent Med'cine; besides the Danger of being killed; it must be own'd that there ought to be a good deal of Discretion had when we use it.

text: Whenever you shall be inclined to consult the Sacred Oracles, from whence the above threatenings are extracted, you will find doctrines and texts, which a truly penitent and contrite heart may lay hold of for its consolation.

text: Believe me, Sirs, that I would not, if I might, choose to live, altho' the pleasantest part of my life were to come over again: And yet Eighteen years of it, out of Nineteen, have been very pleasant.

text: Like or resembling Miss Clarissa Harlowe, they now remember to be a praise denoting the highest degree of approveable excellence, with every-one, whatever person, action, or rank, spoken of.

text: I Have heard, with a great deal of surprize, that you have thought fit to throw out some menacing expressions against me.

text: He asked me, who was the author of the two lines I had repeated to him; and made me speak them over again.

text: Weak! weak, indeed, my dearest Belford, said he, and weaker in my mind, if possible, than in my body; and wept bitterly—or I should not thus unman myself.

text: This letter affords a foundation for future consolation to them; but at present it has new-pointed their grief, by making them reflect on their cruelty to so excellent a Daughter, Niece, and Sister.
author: Richardson, Samuel, 1689-1761.
title: Clarissa: Or, the history of a young lady: comprehending the most important concerns of private life. ... Published by the editor of Pamela. ... [pt.7]

text: If I am to be still the most unhappy of men, let your pen, by one line, tell me so.

text: In consideration of which she allows him to recommend four objects yearly to partake of it.—Allows, is her style; for she assumes the whole prerogative of dispensing this charity; the only prerogative she does or has occasion to assume.
author: Richardson, Samuel, 1689-1761.

text: But say not, Jack, that she must leave us yet.—If she recover—And if I can but re-obtain her favour, then indeed will life be life to me.—The world never saw such an husband as I will make.

title: Clarissa: Or, the history of a young lady: comprehending the most important concerns of private life. ... Published by the editor of Pamela. ... [pt.7]

text: And tho' this of it ſelf hath a Tendence to the Diſſolution of the Government, yet there is another more dangerous than this, if it be not look'd to in time: and that is by Popular Factions.
author: Stephens, Edward, d. 1706.
title: Letters and papers concerning some matters in the last Parliament relating to the commou [sic] rights of all the Commnns [sic] of England, fit to be considered in the next, and by all the said Commons

text: I. Whether the ſeveral Members of the Houſe of Commons be not Authoriſed to Sit and Act there, by their reſpective Counties, Cities, and Burroughs, by Indenture under the Hands and Seals of the Principal Electors for themſelves and the reſt, as Deputies and Truſtees for them all?
author: Stephens, Edward, d. 1706.
title: Letters and papers concerning some matters in the last Parliament relating to the commou [sic] rights of all the Commnns [sic] of England, fit to be considered in the next, and by all the said Commons

text: For they are very few who act upon ſound and ſolid Judgment, but moſt upon common Opinion, receiv'd by Education, taken up upon inconſiderate Apprehenſion, or impos'd upon them by the Craſt and Subtlety of deſigning Men, who abuſe their Hopes and Confidence only to ſerve themſelves.
author: Stephens, Edward, d. 1706.
title: Letters and papers concerning some matters in the last Parliament relating to the commou [sic] rights of all the Commnns [sic] of England, fit to be considered in the next, and by all the said Commons

text: How near have ſuch Factions gone to inſlave the Nation, and ſet up the Monarchy to be Abſolute and Arbitrary?
author: Stephens, Edward, d. 1706.
title: Letters and papers concerning some matters in the last Parliament relating to the commou [sic] rights of all the Commnns [sic] of England, fit to be considered in the next, and by all the said Commons

text: And in ſome I have known a certain and manifeſt Cauſe, and I doubt not, but there was the like in others, but unknown to any but ſuch as would not diſcover it.
author: Stephens, Edward, d. 1706.
title: Letters and papers concerning some matters in the last Parliament relating to the commou [sic] rights of all the Commnns [sic] of England, fit to be considered in the next, and by all the said Commons

text: And whole Families have I known brought to Deſolation, in ſuch manner as ſeemed very plain to me, to be by the ſecret Operations of ſome inviſible intelligent Powers, or ſome Secret Curſe, which did adhere to them, or both.
author: Stephens, Edward, d. 1706.
title: Letters and papers concerning some matters in the last Parliament relating to the commou [sic] rights of all the Commnns [sic] of England, fit to be considered in the next, and by all the said Commons

text: What ſuch things may come to in time, if neglected, no man knows; but what may be done to prevent the Miſchief, is fit to be conſidered.
author: Stephens, Edward, d. 1706.
title: Letters and papers concerning some matters in the last Parliament relating to the commou [sic] rights of all the Commnns [sic] of England, fit to be considered in the next, and by all the said Commons

text: And as for Sir Richard Cox, I had by a former Letter imminded him of the former Caſe; but it ſeems he was not ſo much concerned for your Rights, as ever to move any thing concerning that.
author: Stephens, Edward, d. 1706.
title: Letters and papers concerning some matters in the last Parliament relating to the commou [sic] rights of all the Commnns [sic] of England, fit to be considered in the next, and by all the said Commons

text: Theſe are great Obligations, and ſuch as I cannot diſcharge without taking notice and complaining of what I obſerve greatly amiſs in Both Houſes of Parliament.
author: Stephens, Edward, d. 1706.
title: Letters and papers concerning some matters in the last Parliament relating to the commou [sic] rights of all the Commnns [sic] of England, fit to be considered in the next, and by all the said Commons

text: And when I have asked, why no body moved the Houſe that ſome of them might be called to the Bar, and made Examples, the common Anſwer hath been, It would be to no purpoſe.
author: Stephens, Edward, d. 1706.
title: Letters and papers concerning some matters in the last Parliament relating to the commou [sic] rights of all the Commnns [sic] of England, fit to be considered in the next, and by all the said Commons

text: The true Engliſh Government is both in it ſelf one of the beſt Conſtitutions in the World, and moſt accomodate to the Nature and Genius of the Engliſh People.
author: Stephens, Edward, d. 1706.
title: Letters and papers concerning some matters in the last Parliament relating to the commou [sic] rights of all the Commnns [sic] of England, fit to be considered in the next, and by all the said Commons

text: V. Whether it be not a Breach of Truſt in any ſuch Deputy or Repreſentative not to perform what is ſo required honeſtly and faithfully?

text: But I doubt theſe Politicians do but egregiouſly befool themſelves with a vain Conceit add Preſumption of having the Purſe of the Nation.

text: Theſe ample and full Aſſurances which His Majeſty has in His Letter given you, are ſo diſtinctly expreſſed in it, and in the Diſcourſe the Commiſſioners Grace has had to you, that it were ſuperfluous to me to add much to what you have heard.
author: Marchmont, Patrick Hume, Earl of, 1641-1724.
title: The speech of Patrick Earl of Marchmont, , Lord High Chancellor to the Parliament of Scotland on Tuesday 29 October 1700.

text: By theſe ſeven Channels, His Majeſty is diſpoſed and ready to let out unto this Nation a Stream of moſt valuable Advantages, which cannot miſs (by the Bleſſing of GOD) to make it happy.
author: Marchmont, Patrick Hume, Earl of, 1641-1724.
title: The speech of Patrick Earl of Marchmont, , Lord High Chancellor to the Parliament of Scotland on Tuesday 29 October 1700.

text: Since that time, His Majeſty by a Letter to His Privy Council, publiſhed by his Order, for the Satisfaction of His Good Subjects, has repeated the ſame Aſſurances which were formerly given you, and has expreſſed his good Intentions towards this Kingdom.
author: Marchmont, Patrick Hume, Earl of, 1641-1724.
title: The speech of Patrick Earl of Marchmont, , Lord High Chancellor to the Parliament of Scotland on Tuesday 29 October 1700.

text: Theſe plain Reaſons, I do not doubt, will ſatisfie all theſe who are ſatisfiable, & not too indifferent of keeping up a mutual Truſt and Confidence betwixt His Majeſtie and his People and Parliament.
author: Marchmont, Patrick Hume, Earl of, 1641-1724.
title: The speech of Patrick Earl of Marchmont, , Lord High Chancellor to the Parliament of Scotland on Tuesday 29 October 1700.

text: His Majeſtie is reſolved to give the Royal Aſſent to all Acts for the better eſtabliſhing the true Proteſtant Religion and the Presbyterian Government of the Church which we Enjoy.
author: Marchmont, Patrick Hume, Earl of, 1641-1724.
title: The speech of Patrick Earl of Marchmont, , Lord High Chancellor to the Parliament of Scotland on Tuesday 29 October 1700.

text: Let not the humor or jealouſie of any who have acceſs to the doing Buſineſs in this Juncture, hinder or obſtruct ſo great a Bleſſing as we have in proſpect.
author: Marchmont, Patrick Hume, Earl of, 1641-1724.
title: The speech of Patrick Earl of Marchmont, , Lord High Chancellor to the Parliament of Scotland on Tuesday 29 October 1700.

text: As you have great Aſſurances and Kind offers from your Soveraign at this time, whereby this Nation may be made very happy, its moſt important Intereſts furder ſecured, its Peace preſerved, and its Trade advanced.
author: Marchmont, Patrick Hume, Earl of, 1641-1724.
title: The speech of Patrick Earl of Marchmont, , Lord High Chancellor to the Parliament of Scotland on Tuesday 29 October 1700.

text: Only I muſt much take notice, and I wiſh that you may do ſo too, of the large extent of His Majeſties good Intentions towards his Subjects of this Kingdom.
author: Marchmont, Patrick Hume, Earl of, 1641-1724.
title: The speech of Patrick Earl of Marchmont, , Lord High Chancellor to the Parliament of Scotland on Tuesday 29 October 1700.

text: Now again His Majeſty by His moſt Gracious Letter Read in your Audience, is pleaſed fully and kindly to certifie you, that he continues firm in the ſame good Intentions, ſtill reckoning the Eaſe and Proſperity of His good Subjects to be His greateſt Honor and Happineſs.
author: Marchmont, Patrick Hume, Earl of, 1641-1724.
title: The speech of Patrick Earl of Marchmont, , Lord High Chancellor to the Parliament of Scotland on Tuesday 29 October 1700.

text: That it would infallibly diſturb the general Peace of Chriſtendome, and bring inevitably upon this Kingdom a heavy War, wherein we could expect no aſſiſtance.
author: Marchmont, Patrick Hume, Earl of, 1641-1724.
title: The speech of Patrick Earl of Marchmont, , Lord High Chancellor to the Parliament of Scotland on Tuesday 29 October 1700.

text: There is one thing which has made a difference of Opinion amongſt us, ſome would have an Act aſſerting the Right of the Company to the Colony, which it planted upon Darien.
author: Marchmont, Patrick Hume, Earl of, 1641-1724.
title: The speech of Patrick Earl of Marchmont, , Lord High Chancellor to the Parliament of Scotland on Tuesday 29 October 1700.

text: This is very evident, for the power of the Spaniſh Monarchy, and of thoſe concerned in the Support of it, would be united againſt us, and we in all appearance left to our own ſtrength, without expectation of any Aſſiſtants.
author: Marchmont, Patrick Hume, Earl of, 1641-1724.
title: The speech of Patrick Earl of Marchmont, , Lord High Chancellor to the Parliament of Scotland on Tuesday 29 October 1700.

text: NOW We ſee the Eſtates of this Kingdom again met in Parliament, ſo ſoon as the Kings other weighty Affairs, and his abſence from Britain could allow it; whereby all may be ſatisfied that the Suſpicions which have been vented, as if their Meeting would be delayed and put off, were altogether groundleſs.
author: Marchmont, Patrick Hume, Earl of, 1641-1724.
title: The speech of Patrick Earl of Marchmont, , Lord High Chancellor to the Parliament of Scotland on Tuesday 29 October 1700.

text: Our sex's chief lustre, I own, it obscures: But think what a lesson it offers to yours!

text: But Daphnis to his Fate with Pleaſure run, He ſaw the Nymph, he lov'd, and was undone.
author: Froud, John.
title: Daphnis or, a pastoral elegy upon the unfortunate and much-lamented death of Mr. Thomas Creech.

text: The weeping Heav'ns a Shower of Tears diſtill'd, And all the Woods were with loud Sorrow fill'd. Whilſt mournful Ecchoes all their Sighs rebound, Wiſhing they had been ſomething more than Sound.
author: Froud, John.
title: Daphnis or, a pastoral elegy upon the unfortunate and much-lamented death of Mr. Thomas Creech.

text: But 'tis in vain to ask; 'twas ſo decreed, So I coy Syrnix chas'd, and caught a trembling Reed.
author: Froud, John.
title: Daphnis or, a pastoral elegy upon the unfortunate and much-lamented death of Mr. Thomas Creech.

text: Ah cruel Nymph! we've loſt the learned'ſt Swain That ever ſung on our Arcadia's Plain: What ſprightly Thoughts, what Joy did he inſpire!
author: Froud, John.
title: Daphnis or, a pastoral elegy upon the unfortunate and much-lamented death of Mr. Thomas Creech.

text: Here did the Swains their mournful Theme give o're, Sighs ſtopt their Words, and they could ſpeak no more.
author: Froud, John.
title: Daphnis or, a pastoral elegy upon the unfortunate and much-lamented death of Mr. Thomas Creech.

text: Ungentle Nymph, to thee we owe his Death, 'Twas LALAGE that rob'd poor Daphnis of his Breath.
author: Froud, John.
title: Daphnis or, a pastoral elegy upon the unfortunate and much-lamented death of Mr. Thomas Creech.

text: On you we Gaze, and feel a pleaſing Pain Steal to our Hearts, and glide thro' every Vein.
author: Froud, John.
title: Daphnis or, a pastoral elegy upon the unfortunate and much-lamented death of Mr. Thomas Creech.

text: But thou canſt ne're return— For thou haſt croſt the irreameable Lake, And Charon's Boat comes always empty back.
author: Froud, John.
title: Daphnis or, a pastoral elegy upon the unfortunate and much-lamented death of Mr. Thomas Creech.

text: Fair Fatal Sex! who can our Souls ſurprize With tender Looks, and ſoft bewitching Eyes, Were you but half as pitiful and kind, The God of Love had not been counted blind.
author: Froud, John.
title: Daphnis or, a pastoral elegy upon the unfortunate and much-lamented death of Mr. Thomas Creech.

text: As Hebrus ſtopt for Grief his golden Side, When on it's Banks the tuneful Orpheus dy'd; So do our Groves, and Rivers ſeem to mourn, In ſilent Sorrow, for their Swains return.
author: Froud, John.
title: Daphnis or, a pastoral elegy upon the unfortunate and much-lamented death of Mr. Thomas Creech.

text: Farewel ye Streams, and conſcious Groves, he cry'd: So did the dreadful work of Fate, and dy'd.
author: Froud, John.
title: Daphnis or, a pastoral elegy upon the unfortunate and much-lamented death of Mr. Thomas Creech.

text: Then from our Groves to yonder Wood he flies, (Strange Power of Love!) and there deſpairing dies.
author: Froud, John.
title: Daphnis or, a pastoral elegy upon the unfortunate and much-lamented death of Mr. Thomas Creech.

text: It is no wonder if the whole Nation abound in Infidelity, and all kind of Wickedneſs, when there is no more Religion in thoſe who ſhould correct it among the Commons, and the Latitudinarian Biſhops among the Lords.
author: Stephens, Edward, d. 1706.
title: To the knights, gentlemen and free-holders and commons of England, Edward Stephens wisheth prudence, piety, peace and happiness.

text: But I doubt theſe Politicians do but egregiouſly befool themſelves with a vain Conceit add Preſumption of having the Purſe of the Nation.
author: Stephens, Edward, d. 1706.
title: To the knights, gentlemen and free-holders and commons of England, Edward Stephens wisheth prudence, piety, peace and happiness.

text: And if we do not appear as well for the Honour of the King, when there is occaſion, as for the Rights of the Subject, we do not diſcharge our Duty to our Country, perform our Oath to the King, or are Worthy of the Benefit of ſo Noble a Government.
author: Stephens, Edward, d. 1706.
title: To the knights, gentlemen and free-holders and commons of England, Edward Stephens wisheth prudence, piety, peace and happiness.

text: And I ſhall do it firſt to you, as my proper Repreſentative; and by you deſire it may be repreſented to the Houſe, as you will anſwer it to your Country, for which you ſerve.
author: Stephens, Edward, d. 1706.
title: To the knights, gentlemen and free-holders and commons of England, Edward Stephens wisheth prudence, piety, peace and happiness.

text: WHat you ſee here Open was ſent Sealed to divers Members, your Truſtees and Repreſentatives in Parliament, being then printed, not to be publiſh'd, but only a ſmall number to be preſented to them.
author: Stephens, Edward, d. 1706.
title: To the knights, gentlemen and free-holders and commons of England, Edward Stephens wisheth prudence, piety, peace and happiness.

text: AS I am a Commoner of England, it is, as I told you before, my Right and my Duty to take notice, and complain to the Houſe of Commons, of all, or any ſuch matters of publick Concern as are proper for the Inquiry or Conſideration of that Houſe.
author: Stephens, Edward, d. 1706.
title: To the knights, gentlemen and free-holders and commons of England, Edward Stephens wisheth prudence, piety, peace and happiness.

text: For theſe things I appeal to the Righteous Judgment of Almighty God, to your own Conſciences, and to the next Parliamant; and to a Convention of the Clergy, as to what concerns the Biſhops and the falſe Charge of Popery.
author: Stephens, Edward, d. 1706.
title: To the knights, gentlemen and free-holders and commons of England, Edward Stephens wisheth prudence, piety, peace and happiness.

text: And beſides all this, I am obliged by Oath to be faithful to the preſent King, which I intend, by the Grace of God, faithfully to perform, tho for ſpecial, and, I think, good Reaſons, I refuſe to take it again.
author: Stephens, Edward, d. 1706.
title: To the knights, gentlemen and free-holders and commons of England, Edward Stephens wisheth prudence, piety, peace and happiness.

text: Theſe are great Obligations, and ſuch as I cannot diſcharge without taking notice and complaining of what I obſerve greatly amiſs in Both Houſes of Parliament.
author: Stephens, Edward, d. 1706.
title: To the knights, gentlemen and free-holders and commons of England, Edward Stephens wisheth prudence, piety, peace and happiness.

text: And when I have asked, why no body moved the Houſe that ſome of them might be called to the Bar, and made Examples, the common Anſwer hath been, It would be to no purpoſe.
author: Stephens, Edward, d. 1706.
title: To the knights, gentlemen and free-holders and commons of England, Edward Stephens wisheth prudence, piety, peace and happiness.

text: How ſuch things can be conſiſtent either with Conſcience and Religion, Civil Duty to our Country, and one of the beſt Governments in the World, or their Oaths of Fidelity to the King, I do not underſtand: Nor ſo much as with common Prudence for themſelves, and their own Rights.
author: Stephens, Edward, d. 1706.
title: To the knights, gentlemen and free-holders and commons of England, Edward Stephens wisheth prudence, piety, peace and happiness.

text: But beſides all this, I have been for ſome Years, by the ſpecial Providence of Almighty God, engaged in his more immediate Service, and without limitation to any ſpecial Charge; ſo that where-ever I have opportunity for his Service, I am obliged faithfully to diſcharge it.
author: Stephens, Edward, d. 1706.
title: To the knights, gentlemen and free-holders and commons of England, Edward Stephens wisheth prudence, piety, peace and happiness.

text: Nay, ſhould the King but diſſolve this Parliament, and in a Declaration ſet out ſuch Reaſons as he may for that, and for Calling of another, their little Politicks with themſelves might probably be ſoon in the dirt.
author: Stephens, Edward, d. 1706.
title: To the knights, gentlemen and free-holders and commons of England, Edward Stephens wisheth prudence, piety, peace and happiness.

text: The preſent Life is to the moſt faithful Servants of Chriſt, for the moſt part, a ſtate of hardſhip, for 'tis a perpetual warfare.
author: Knight, John, 1651-1712.
title: A sermon preach'd at the funeral of The Right Honourable the Lady Guilford, Nov. 18, 1699 by John Knight ...

text: Her bodily Structure was Beautiful and Exact, which being ſuitably informed and animated by a Devout Soul, added to her the further Ornament of a moſt chaſt Converſation.
author: Knight, John, 1651-1712.
title: A sermon preach'd at the funeral of The Right Honourable the Lady Guilford, Nov. 18, 1699 by John Knight ...

text: When the Righteous dye there is a full end of all their Troubles: Death is their laſt Enemy, and he diſarmed, that he can ſting no more.
author: Knight, John, 1651-1712.
title: A sermon preach'd at the funeral of The Right Honourable the Lady Guilford, Nov. 18, 1699 by John Knight ...

text: To her Servants and Dependants She was a Nurſing Mother; to her Acquaintance an obliging Friend; and to all her Relatives and Allies, She even exceeded in Tenderneſs and Affection.
author: Knight, John, 1651-1712.
title: A sermon preach'd at the funeral of The Right Honourable the Lady Guilford, Nov. 18, 1699 by John Knight ...

text: For She would never put up an Affront offer'd to God or Religion, without ſhewing her Reſentments, which could not but gain her ſuch an inward Eſteem, among all People of Worth or Honour, as more than compenſated for what She loſt of outward Complement and Reſpect, from ſome other Perſons.
author: Knight, John, 1651-1712.
title: A sermon preach'd at the funeral of The Right Honourable the Lady Guilford, Nov. 18, 1699 by John Knight ...

text: Were there then any Prophecies to this purpoſe, which Holy Men of old ſpoke, as they were moved by the Holy Ghoſt?
author: Knight, John, 1651-1712.
title: A sermon preach'd at the funeral of The Right Honourable the Lady Guilford, Nov. 18, 1699 by John Knight ...

text: Theſe poor Creatures it ſeems, in any manner of Diſtreſs, very ordinarily, with Saul apply themſelves to Witches and Inchantments for Relief.
author: Knight, John, 1651-1712.
title: A sermon preach'd at the funeral of The Right Honourable the Lady Guilford, Nov. 18, 1699 by John Knight ...

text: This is certain; By theſe fatherly Diſciplines She was trained up, and admirably accompliſh'd for the diſcharge of her Duty in all thoſe Stations and Relations the Divine Providence had appointed her to ſuſtain.
author: Knight, John, 1651-1712.
title: A sermon preach'd at the funeral of The Right Honourable the Lady Guilford, Nov. 18, 1699 by John Knight ...

text: They have innumerable Enemies, and theſe for the moſt part in ambuſcade: The ſnares that are laid for them, often give them falls, and then the Bruiſe is long a Curing, and the Operation of the Medicine painful and afflictive.
author: Knight, John, 1651-1712.
title: A sermon preach'd at the funeral of The Right Honourable the Lady Guilford, Nov. 18, 1699 by John Knight ...

text: Then ſhew the neceſſary Connexion there is betwixt his and ours, i. e. Becauſe he is riſen, we ſhall alſo infallibly be rais'd from the dead.
author: Knight, John, 1651-1712.
title: A sermon preach'd at the funeral of The Right Honourable the Lady Guilford, Nov. 18, 1699 by John Knight ...

text: To die the death of Kings, or Stateſmen, was too ſtupid a wiſh even for ſuch a Man as Balaam.
author: Knight, John, 1651-1712.
title: A sermon preach'd at the funeral of The Right Honourable the Lady Guilford, Nov. 18, 1699 by John Knight ...

text: And if they find any ſuch, they muſt in ſpight of their Teeth confeſs, that the Accompliſhment of them is an immoveable Teſtimony to the Foreknowledge and Wiſdom, to the infinite Power and Truth of God.
author: Knight, John, 1651-1712.
title: A sermon preach'd at the funeral of The Right Honourable the Lady Guilford, Nov. 18, 1699 by John Knight ...

text: To forward her growth in theſe Attainments, She was not a little obliged to the Gifts of Nature, tho' much more to the Divine Grace; as we are allowed to diſtinguiſh, tho' 'tis all of Grace.
author: Knight, John, 1651-1712.
title: A sermon preach'd at the funeral of The Right Honourable the Lady Guilford, Nov. 18, 1699 by John Knight ...

text: It reasons from what it sees on the surface of the earth, but it does not carry itself on to the solar system existing by motion.
author: Paine, Thomas, 1737-1809.
title: Atheism refuted: in a discourse to prove the existence of a God.

text: But infidelity by ascribing every phenomenon to properties of matter, conceives a system for which it cannot account, and yet it pretends to demonstration.
author: Paine, Thomas, 1737-1809.
title: Atheism refuted: in a discourse to prove the existence of a God.

text: And when we speak of looking through nature up to nature's God, we speak philosophically the same rational language as when we speak of looking through human laws up to the power that ordained them.
author: Paine, Thomas, 1737-1809.
title: Atheism refuted: in a discourse to prove the existence of a God.

text: How then is it, that when we study the works of God in the Creation, we stop short and do not think of God?
author: Paine, Thomas, 1737-1809.
title: Atheism refuted: in a discourse to prove the existence of a God.

text: Every thing which has hitherto been discovered with respect to the motion of the planets in the system, relates only to the laws by which motion acts, and not to the cause of motion.
author: Paine, Thomas, 1737-1809.
title: Atheism refuted: in a discourse to prove the existence of a God.

text: When this simple idea presents itself to our mind we have the idea of a perfect being that man calls God.
author: Paine, Thomas, 1737-1809.
title: Atheism refuted: in a discourse to prove the existence of a God.

text: But the motion that upholds the solar system is of an entire different kind, and is not a property of matter.
author: Paine, Thomas, 1737-1809.
title: Atheism refuted: in a discourse to prove the existence of a God.

text: As to that which is called nature, it is no other than the laws by which motion and action of every kind, with respect to unintelligible matter, is regulated.
author: Paine, Thomas, 1737-1809.
title: Atheism refuted: in a discourse to prove the existence of a God.

text: It sees that an oak produces an acorn, an acorn an oak, a bird an egg, an egg a bird, and so on.
author: Paine, Thomas, 1737-1809.
title: Atheism refuted: in a discourse to prove the existence of a God.

text: To him we hold out this universe as a thing that man could not make; to him we propose it as the evidence for his belief, as the inimitable word of God.
author: Paine, Thomas, 1737-1809.
title: Atheism refuted: in a discourse to prove the existence of a God.

text: If we unite to the present instruction, a series of lectures on the ground I have mentioned, we shall, in the first place, render theology the most delightful, and entertaining of all studies.
author: Paine, Thomas, 1737-1809.
title: Atheism refuted: in a discourse to prove the existence of a God.

text: The one perverts the sublime and enlightening study of natural philosophy into a deformity of absurdities by not reasoning to the end; the other loses himself in the obscurity of metaphysical theories, and dishonours the Creator by treating the study of his works with contempt.
author: Paine, Thomas, 1737-1809.
title: Atheism refuted: in a discourse to prove the existence of a God.

text: The one is a half-rational of whom there is some hope, the other a visionary to whom we must be charitable.
author: Paine, Thomas, 1737-1809.
title: Atheism refuted: in a discourse to prove the existence of a God.

text: But now as I look o'er thy bowers, As each shrub, and each stream, I survey, Disaster invades the soft flowers: For—oh—their lov'd master's away.
author: Pratt, Mr. (Samuel Jackson), 1749-1814.
title: The tears of genius: Occasioned by the death of Dr. Goldsmith. By Courtney Melmoth.

text: And rises then my sorrow into guilt, Verges my fondness on impiety, Reason, religion, duty, all forgot?
author: Pratt, Mr. (Samuel Jackson), 1749-1814.
title: The tears of genius: Occasioned by the death of Dr. Goldsmith. By Courtney Melmoth.

text: And oh (she cried with frantic grief) Who now shall bring relief, Or where the cordial shall I find, To soothe a mother's mind, Since LYTTELTON is dead?
author: Pratt, Mr. (Samuel Jackson), 1749-1814.
title: The tears of genius: Occasioned by the death of Dr. Goldsmith. By Courtney Melmoth.

text: Long shall the Muses mourn their pensive friend, Long shall a mother's bosom throb with woe, O'er his lov'd tomb the duteous swains shall bend, And Albion's daughters long bewail the blow.
author: Pratt, Mr. (Samuel Jackson), 1749-1814.
title: The tears of genius: Occasioned by the death of Dr. Goldsmith. By Courtney Melmoth.

text: How shall I paint the glories of his mind, Benevolent, and kind, His reason strong, and elegantly clear, To every virtue dear!
author: Pratt, Mr. (Samuel Jackson), 1749-1814.
title: The tears of genius: Occasioned by the death of Dr. Goldsmith. By Courtney Melmoth.

text: Beyond the common flight of modern song, Beyond the tinsel of the rhimeing tribe, Which for the flimsy Sonnet cull the flowers Parnassian (scarce deserving to be cropt, The stinted scyons of the mountain's foot) To deck their May-day garland of an hour.
author: Pratt, Mr. (Samuel Jackson), 1749-1814.
title: The tears of genius: Occasioned by the death of Dr. Goldsmith. By Courtney Melmoth.

text: Full gentle, and sweet, was the note That flow'd from his delicate heart, Simplicity, smil'd as he wrote, And Nature was polish'd by art.
author: Pratt, Mr. (Samuel Jackson), 1749-1814.
title: The tears of genius: Occasioned by the death of Dr. Goldsmith. By Courtney Melmoth.

text: Oh! fall severely felt, To make a parent melt, The tender breast to tear; And wake despair: And scarce a child the mighty grief to share!
author: Pratt, Mr. (Samuel Jackson), 1749-1814.
title: The tears of genius: Occasioned by the death of Dr. Goldsmith. By Courtney Melmoth.

text: And now, my lov'd Shenstone, for Thee, Thou pride of the pastoral strain; Thou fairest resemblance of me, Dear, elegant Bard of the plain.
author: Pratt, Mr. (Samuel Jackson), 1749-1814.
title: The tears of genius: Occasioned by the death of Dr. Goldsmith. By Courtney Melmoth.

text: Tho' the grav'd tomb, and cloud aspiring bust To Cam's clear margin, call not back thy breath, Yet shall fair Fame immortalize thy dust, And GENIUS snatch thee from the realms of death.
author: Pratt, Mr. (Samuel Jackson), 1749-1814.
title: The tears of genius: Occasioned by the death of Dr. Goldsmith. By Courtney Melmoth.

text: I almost mingle blushes with my woe, Confusion flings her crimson in my cheek, And colouring Conscience dyes a deeper red!
author: Pratt, Mr. (Samuel Jackson), 1749-1814.
title: The tears of genius: Occasioned by the death of Dr. Goldsmith. By Courtney Melmoth.

text: GOLDSMITH adieu! the "book-learn'd priest" for thee Shall now in vain possess his festive glee, The oft-heard jest in vain he shall reveal, For now alas, the jest he cannot feel.
author: Pratt, Mr. (Samuel Jackson), 1749-1814.
title: The tears of genius: Occasioned by the death of Dr. Goldsmith. By Courtney Melmoth.

text: Here low in dust, a son of Science lies, By fame distinguished, and to Genius dear; Forgive the fault, ye cynically wise, If on his grave the parent sheds a tear.
author: Pratt, Mr. (Samuel Jackson), 1749-1814.
title: The tears of genius: Occasioned by the death of Dr. Goldsmith. By Courtney Melmoth.

text: The Bodies ſhall be no longer neither a Wall, nor a Vail between God and the Souls, nor a Channel of Communication between the Souls and God: He will Act in them independently of the Diſpoſition of the Body, which is now the eſſential Condition of his natural Action in us.
author: C. B., D.D.
title: A discovery of divine mysteries, or, The nature and efficacy of the soul of man considered in all its faculties, operations and divine perfections, and how it governs in divine and secular affairs of

text: It would be very ill to underſtand Chriſtian Morality and the Goſpel, to regard it as a malignant Inclination and a Jealouſie which God hath of us, to grudge us our little Pleaſure, and our Natural Satisfaction.
author: C. B., D.D.
title: A discovery of divine mysteries, or, The nature and efficacy of the soul of man considered in all its faculties, operations and divine perfections, and how it governs in divine and secular affairs of

text: And who do's not ſee, if it be ſo, that there is no means of granting Beaſts Inſtincts to enlighten them, ſince they do not enlighten us our ſelves, who are otherwiſe undiſputably capable of being enlightned by Reaſon.
author: C. B., D.D.
title: A discovery of divine mysteries, or, The nature and efficacy of the soul of man considered in all its faculties, operations and divine perfections, and how it governs in divine and secular affairs of

text: God doth not deny Us any Pleaſure for the Pleaſure's ſake; but he hath inclos'd this Rivulet and this Current within its Banks and its Channel; He hath preſcribed certain Bounds and certain Circumſtances to it, beyond which he will not have it paſs.
author: C. B., D.D.
title: A discovery of divine mysteries, or, The nature and efficacy of the soul of man considered in all its faculties, operations and divine perfections, and how it governs in divine and secular affairs of

text: They are neither Miſtreſſes of Health nor Sickneſs: Health and Sickneſs are in Us by an Invincible and an Almighty Empire of Nature; Fevers, Apoplexies, Collicks, and Dyſenteries, neither ask our Leaves to attack us, nor our Agreement to march off.
author: C. B., D.D.
title: A discovery of divine mysteries, or, The nature and efficacy of the soul of man considered in all its faculties, operations and divine perfections, and how it governs in divine and secular affairs of

text: You ſee there the general Idea of Senſation, which are the Knowledges that we have by the Determination of preſent Objects.
author: C. B., D.D.
title: A discovery of divine mysteries, or, The nature and efficacy of the soul of man considered in all its faculties, operations and divine perfections, and how it governs in divine and secular affairs of

text: We are his Images in Nature, that we may be his Images alſo in Glory: For it is not in vain, that we are the Portraiture, and the lively animated Picture of that Supream and Eternal Nature, in the Foundation of the Eſſence of our Souls.
author: C. B., D.D.
title: A discovery of divine mysteries, or, The nature and efficacy of the soul of man considered in all its faculties, operations and divine perfections, and how it governs in divine and secular affairs of

text: God hath rough-drawn the Table, ſaith St. Auguſtin; and then he hath put into our hands the Pencil and the Colours; and he hath given us all our Life-time to compleat and finiſh it.
author: C. B., D.D.
title: A discovery of divine mysteries, or, The nature and efficacy of the soul of man considered in all its faculties, operations and divine perfections, and how it governs in divine and secular affairs of

text: What they judge of all that Train of Myſteries and Miracles which makes the Body of that which we call the Holy Hiſtory, or the Hiſtory of Religion?
author: C. B., D.D.
title: A discovery of divine mysteries, or, The nature and efficacy of the soul of man considered in all its faculties, operations and divine perfections, and how it governs in divine and secular affairs of

text: At that time when we judg'd that Beaſts knew like us, this falſe and raſh Judgment was divided, and as it were ſpread into four different Opinions.
author: C. B., D.D.
title: A discovery of divine mysteries, or, The nature and efficacy of the soul of man considered in all its faculties, operations and divine perfections, and how it governs in divine and secular affairs of

text: They are only but Acceſſorily, if I may ſo ſay, either in Heaven or in Hell, within theſe Material Places and Spaces, of which, God gives them that lively Idea, which renders Them preſent to them.
author: C. B., D.D.
title: A discovery of divine mysteries, or, The nature and efficacy of the soul of man considered in all its faculties, operations and divine perfections, and how it governs in divine and secular affairs of

text: But perhaps our Souls, having once been loſt, may be Redeem'd again; but who do's not know that with Pain God Redeem'd them once?
author: C. B., D.D.
title: A discovery of divine mysteries, or, The nature and efficacy of the soul of man considered in all its faculties, operations and divine perfections, and how it governs in divine and secular affairs of

text: The Soul is undervalu'd and forgotten in general, they ſacrifice it every moment to the Body; and this Order of Preference, which is ſo lawfully due, cannot be more ſubverted; But this is not a place to go on with the Invective, let us paſs unto other Duties.
author: C. B., D.D.
title: A discovery of divine mysteries, or, The nature and efficacy of the soul of man considered in all its faculties, operations and divine perfections, and how it governs in divine and secular affairs of

title: The just limitation of slavery: in the laws of God, compared with the unbounded claims of the African traders and British American slaveholders. By Granville Sharp. With a copious appendix: ...

text: Thou shalt not oppress a Stranger; for ye know the heart of a stranger, seeing ye were strangers in the land of Egypt.
author: Sharp, Granville, 1735-1813.

text: THIS, Sir, is my opinion concerning the people in question, which I submit to your consideration, merely as matter of opinion: for I cannot pretend to speak with certainty.

text: Here the dire locusts horrid swarms prevail; Here the blue asps with livid poison swell; Here the dry dipsa wriths his sinuous mail; O can we not here, secure from envy, dwell?
author: Sharp, Granville, 1735-1813.
title: The just limitation of slavery: in the laws of God, compared with the unbounded claims of the African traders and British American slaveholders. By Granville Sharp. With a copious appendix: ...

text: 'IN another place they observe,' since we are all brethren, and God has given to all men a natural right to Liberty, we allow of no Slavery among us, unless a person forfeits his freedom by his crimes.

text: In Fortune's Car behold that Minion ride, With either India's glittering Spoils opprest: So moves the Sumpter-Mule, in harness'd Pride, That bears the Treasure which he cannot taste.
author: Smollett, Tobias George, 1721-1771.
title: Independence: an ode. By the late T. Smollet, M.D:

text: He, with the generous Rustics, sate On Uri's Rocks in close Divan; And wing'd that Arrow sure as Fate, Which ascertain'd the sacred Rights of Man.
author: Smollett, Tobias George, 1721-1771.
title: Independence: an ode. By the late T. Smollet, M.D:

text: The Saxon Prince in Horror fled From Altars stain'd with human Gore; And Liberty his routed Legions led In Safety to the bleak Norwegian Shore.
author: Smollett, Tobias George, 1721-1771.
title: Independence: an ode. By the late T. Smollet, M.D:

text: There in a Cave asleep she lay, Lull'd by the hoarse-resounding Main; When a bold Savage past that Way, Impell'd by Destiny, his Name Disdain.
author: Smollett, Tobias George, 1721-1771.
title: Independence: an ode. By the late T. Smollet, M.D:

text: Of ample Front the portly Chief appear'd: The hunted Bear supplied a shaggy Vest; The drifted Snow hung on his yellow Beard; And his broad Shoulders brav'd the furious Blast.
author: Smollett, Tobias George, 1721-1771.
title: Independence: an ode. By the late T. Smollet, M.D:

text: No, Sir; but there is some News from the Secretaries Office, a Mail is arrived from Holland, and you will have the Contents of it in one of the Evening Papers.
author: Fielding, Henry, 1707-1754.
title: The coffee-house politician: or, the justice caught in his own trap. A comedy. As it is acted at the Theatre-Royal in Lincoln's-Inn Fields. Written by Mr. Fielding.

text: Yet I must own the Girl hath been ever dutiful to me, till she became acquainted with this cursed Fellow in a Red Coat.
author: Fielding, Henry, 1707-1754.
title: The coffee-house politician: or, the justice caught in his own trap. A comedy. As it is acted at the Theatre-Royal in Lincoln's-Inn Fields. Written by Mr. Fielding.

text: For Pity's sake, Sir, secure him; do not let him escape, 'till we send for a Constable.
author: Fielding, Henry, 1707-1754.
title: The coffee-house politician: or, the justice caught in his own trap. A comedy. As it is acted at the Theatre-Royal in Lincoln's-Inn Fields. Written by Mr. Fielding.

text: Not speak against Women! you shall as soon compel me not to drink; you shall sow up my Lips, if you do either—Here, you, let the Punch be gotten ready.
author: Fielding, Henry, 1707-1754.
title: The coffee-house politician: or, the justice caught in his own trap. A comedy. As it is acted at the Theatre-Royal in Lincoln's-Inn Fields. Written by Mr. Fielding.

text: An Intrigue with a rich Justice's Wife, is not to be slighted by a young Fellow of a desperate Fortune.
author: Fielding, Henry, 1707-1754.
title: The coffee-house politician: or, the justice caught in his own trap. A comedy. As it is acted at the Theatre-Royal in Lincoln's-Inn Fields. Written by Mr. Fielding.

text: I have almost forgotten, but I think it was one of the Greek Emperors, or one of the Turks.
author: Fielding, Henry, 1707-1754.
title: The coffee-house politician: or, the justice caught in his own trap. A comedy. As it is acted at the Theatre-Royal in Lincoln's-Inn Fields. Written by Mr. Fielding.

text: Yes, Sir, I had; but I turn'd him out of Doors, and believe he was hanged long ago.
author: Fielding, Henry, 1707-1754.
title: The coffee-house politician: or, the justice caught in his own trap. A comedy. As it is acted at the Theatre-Royal in Lincoln's-Inn Fields. Written by Mr. Fielding.

text: Ha! what's become of thy Wench? if thou hadst none, thy Absence was the more inexcusable.
author: Fielding, Henry, 1707-1754.
title: The coffee-house politician: or, the justice caught in his own trap. A comedy. As it is acted at the Theatre-Royal in Lincoln's-Inn Fields. Written by Mr. Fielding.

text: If thou hadst stood to thy Bottle like an honest Fellow this had never happened, but you must go a Whoring with a Pox to you, at your Years too; with these spindle Shanks, that weezle Face, that Crane's Neck of a Body.
author: Fielding, Henry, 1707-1754.
title: The coffee-house politician: or, the justice caught in his own trap. A comedy. As it is acted at the Theatre-Royal in Lincoln's-Inn Fields. Written by Mr. Fielding.

text: If you do not understand good Usage, while it is dealt you, you may, when you feel the Reverse.
author: Fielding, Henry, 1707-1754.
title: The coffee-house politician: or, the justice caught in his own trap. A comedy. As it is acted at the Theatre-Royal in Lincoln's-Inn Fields. Written by Mr. Fielding.

text: I'll introduce you to some Clubs of my Acquaintance, a set of honest Fellows that live in the Clouds of Tobacco, and know no Home but a Tavern.
author: Fielding, Henry, 1707-1754.
title: The coffee-house politician: or, the justice caught in his own trap. A comedy. As it is acted at the Theatre-Royal in Lincoln's-Inn Fields. Written by Mr. Fielding.

text: I left the Ship wherein she was to dine with the Captain of one of our Convoy, when a sudden violent Storm arising, I lost sight of her Ship, and from that Day have never seen or heard of her.
author: Fielding, Henry, 1707-1754.
title: The coffee-house politician: or, the justice caught in his own trap. A comedy. As it is acted at the Theatre-Royal in Lincoln's-Inn Fields. Written by Mr. Fielding.

text: I would have given all I was worth in the World, to have been here; but since I escaped, let us forget it.
author: Fielding, Henry, 1707-1754.
title: The coffee-house politician: or, the justice caught in his own trap. A comedy. As it is acted at the Theatre-Royal in Lincoln's-Inn Fields. Written by Mr. Fielding.

text: Ariſe, O God; the Lord appears: For on the ſhameleſs Cheek They now are ſmitten with Reproach, That did my Ruin ſeek.
author: Phillips, John, Mr.
title: Daveidos: or, a specimen of some of David's psalms in English metre With remarks upon the late translators, by Mr. John Phillips.

text: He ſav'd me from my ſtrongeſt Foes That bare me deadly Spight, Depriv'd of other Force to ſhun The Preſſure of their Might.
author: Phillips, John, Mr.
title: Daveidos: or, a specimen of some of David's psalms in English metre With remarks upon the late translators, by Mr. John Phillips.

text: The Pangs of Death environ'd me On every ſide diſtreſs'd; The wicked, like the rowling Waves, To my Deſtruction preſs'd. The Chains of Death about my Life Were like a Circle thrown; Entangl'd in the Snares of Death, My hopes were almoſt gone.
author: Phillips, John, Mr.
title: Daveidos: or, a specimen of some of David's psalms in English metre With remarks upon the late translators, by Mr. John Phillips.

text: Chas'd by ſuch Inſtruments of Death, No place ſhall give them Reſt, He makes his Arrows ſharp to pierce The Perſecutor's Breaſt.
author: Phillips, John, Mr.
title: Daveidos: or, a specimen of some of David's psalms in English metre With remarks upon the late translators, by Mr. John Phillips.

text: But he that dwells in Heav'n above, Shall laugh them all to ſcorn; And in deriſion of their Craft, Their Plots to folly turn.
author: Phillips, John, Mr.
title: Daveidos: or, a specimen of some of David's psalms in English metre With remarks upon the late translators, by Mr. John Phillips.

text: For always will he not forget The Poor when they complain, Nor ſhall the Humble in Diſtreſs, For ever wait in vain.
author: Phillips, John, Mr.
title: Daveidos: or, a specimen of some of David's psalms in English metre With remarks upon the late translators, by Mr. John Phillips.

text: He has advanc'd in Fame The Strength of Iſrael, His choſen People They, Who in his Favour dwell.
author: Phillips, John, Mr.
title: Daveidos: or, a specimen of some of David's psalms in English metre With remarks upon the late translators, by Mr. John Phillips.
